La mobilisation citoyenne pour le droit: Citizen Mobilization for the Right to Housing
Face à cette mobilisation, l’arrondissem: Faced with this mobilization, the borough backed down and voted against the project.
Shahedur Rashid Khan, nous raconte comme: Shahedur Rashid Khan tells us how he faced the renovictions planned by the owner of his building, where he has lived for more than 20 years.
Face à la crise du logement qui sévit à: Faced with the housing crisis gripping Montréal, citizens are redoubling their efforts to change the game and assert their rights. Sometimes, against all odds, refusing to give in pays off, as does collective effort. They share their stories with us.
Sur le boulevard de l’Acadie, face à la: On de l’Acadie Boulevard, facing the fence that separates them from the Town of Mount Royal, Parc-Extension residents are celebrating a victory. Thanks to the intervention of the Comité d’action de Parc-Extension (CAPE), the community has gotten its hands on 7965 de l’Acadie, a property that was home to a doctor’s abandoned house. One day, and everyone hopes it will be soon, neighbourhood residents will move into their future homes on this site. CAPE serves as the neighbourhood’s housing committee.
Depuis 1986, l’organisme défend les droi: Since 1986, the organization has defended tenants’ rights, notably by offering training and assistance to the most disadvantaged among them. “We inform them about their rights, and also their obligations, as tenants; we promote social housing and we fight gentrification,” explains Celia Dehouche, a CAPE community worker.
<strong>Le droit de préemption à la resc: The Right of First Refusal to the Rescue
Sur le perron du bungalow en décrépitude: On the porch of the crumbling bungalow, she explains that the coveted lot came very close to falling into the hands of a private developer. In August 2020, the property had been put up for sale by an individual owner and was subject to the City of Montréal’s right of first refusal. “That’s why we fought, we knew the city could buy the land,” says Ms. Dehouche.
Cette mesure donne à la municipalité la: This measure gives the municipality priority to buy the land in order to develop a community project on it. “The acquisition is good news, because it takes the land off the private market. Since it’s no longer possible for a real estate developer to buy it, it limits speculation,” she explains. Despite the power the City has, it is difficult to achieve such a result. “There are bureaucratic obstacles, and there are elected officials who are pressuring for this land to be bought by a private developer.
L’argument, c’est de parler de revitalis: The argument is to talk about revitalization to justify gentrification. They say it brings money into the borough,” says Ms. Dehouche. As soon as 7965 de l’Acadie went up for sale, the neighbourhood mobilized: demonstrations, letters, site occupations – every means was used to pressure the City of Montréal. Although the pandemic slowed their efforts, as residents’ energy was needed elsewhere, those efforts paid off. The fight continues for CAPE, which wants the City of Montréal to exercise its right of first refusal again for another building in the neighbourhood. Acquired by a real estate developer, 700 Jarry was slated to be converted into luxury apartments.
« Les gens étaient très inquiets que cel: “People were very worried that it would speed up gentrification, especially in the north of the neighbourhood,” says Amy Darwish, a CAPE community worker. The neighbours quickly stepped in and, once again, letters opposing the project were sent and demonstrations were organized.
Face à cette mobilisation, l’arrondissem: Faced with this mobilization, the borough backed down and voted against the project. “Because of the widespread opposition, the developer put the site up for sale. We don’t know if it still is at this point. We’re trying to send a very, very clear message that the City absolutely must acquire this site using its right of first refusal,” says the community worker.
Nous ne pensons pas que le quartier puis: We don’t think the neighbourhood can afford to lose another piece of land that could be used to build affordable housing, especially with the pressure tenants are under these days.”
Dès que les fonds pourront être débloqué: As soon as funds can be released, CAPE wants to develop housing on the lots acquired by the City. But, according to the organization, the game is far from won. It is the provincial government that will decide what happens next, through Accès Logis, a program of the Société d’habitation du Québec. The funding allocated to the program determines how many social housing units will be built. The budget announced last spring by Quebec Finance Minister Éric Girard provides an envelope of $250M for the entire province, a sum that would allow the construction of 500 new units from 2022 to 2026. That number does not include 7965 de l’Acadie, or any other new project, despite the acquisition of the land.
Pour la communauté, c’est beaucoup trop: For the community, this is far too little. In Parc-Extension alone, the demand is for 600 housing units for neighbourhood residents. “There’s a lack of investment; at the rate we’re going, according to figures from a FRAPRU study, it will take 145 years to meet the real demand in the city of Montréal,” laments Ms. Dehouche. “If the borough faces cuts, it’s felt directly by the population.”
Pour l’instant, il est impossible de sav: For now, it is impossible to know when the project at 7965 de l’Acadie will take shape. Based on the site’s zoning, projections point to a four-storey building with 22 units of two or three bedrooms. “It would be ideal for families facing eviction,” says Ms. Dehouche.
C’est ce que souhaite voir Abdul, un pèr: That is what Abdul, a father who has lived in the neighbourhood for seven years, hopes to see. “I’m fighting for better housing conditions,” says the young professional, before explaining that affordable housing is non-existent, even when paying more. “I’m a witness to it, I’ve experienced it myself. The ones that are available aren’t livable,” he adds. Abdul is a front-line worker in the pharmaceutical industry. To cope with the pandemic, he founded a support group that, among other things, distributes meals to Parc-Extension residents. He is particularly attached to his neighbourhood. It is where his three children go to school, and it is the place that welcomed him a few months after he arrived in Canada.
« Les gros titres annoncent toujours que: “The headlines always announce that Parc-Extension is being gentrified. Beyond what makes the front page, it’s a warm and unique neighbourhood, distinguished by the strength of its citizens. The only thing we’re concerned about is housing,” he says, before deploring elected officials’ inaction on the issue.
« Selon ma compréhension, le problème es: “From what I understand, the problem is such that none of our political decision-makers, housing commissioners or others are living through a situation like this. They have no idea how people are suffering and how it could be remedied.” Samira, 25, has lived her whole life in Parc-Extension, in the very apartment where she was born. Over the years, she has seen a dozen families come and go in the apartment across from hers. The rent for that unit is nothing like hers. “I count myself lucky, because we’re one of the only families in the neighbourhood with an affordable apartment,” she says.
Elle partage les sentiments d’Abdul au s: She shares Abdul’s feelings about the place where she grew up. The young woman has a vision for the neighbourhood: families who no longer have to worry about paying for their housing (who today sometimes spend more than half their income on rent) and who have access to healthy, decent and safe housing. “No one deserves to be on the street, or to be evicted because of renovations,” says the student, who describes herself as an engaged citizen.
Samira compte vivre encore longtemps ici: Samira plans to live here for a long time. She hopes the neighbourhood’s residents can do the same if they wish. It is an increasingly unlikely possibility if they have to leave the neighbourhood to find more affordable housing elsewhere. “You often hear that Parc-Extension is a neighbourhood of integration. It’s the local resources that help people and make integration easier, like social services, grocery stores and places of worship. If families like mine are told to live far away from the neighbourhood, how will their integration be made easier?” she observes. Always ready to help, Samira mobilizes whenever she can to support a community struggling with housing problems.
Depuis longtemps, elle agit à titre d’in: For a long time, she has acted as an interpreter in disputes, speaking French, English and Bengali. “A lot of people want to be activists, but they first have to ensure their survival,” says the student. She encourages all the neighbourhood’s residents to go to demonstrations and meetings and to sign petitions. “I want people’s voices to be heard, even those of people who can’t be there,” she says.

Confortablement assis dans son salon sur: Comfortably seated in his living room on a black leather sofa, Shahedur Rashid Khan is at home, and feels at ease. In the room, a work desk is adorned with decorations made by his children, along with his son’s small aquarium, where little translucent fish swim quietly. On the wall hang golden garlands made by his daughter for Eid al-Fitr. Everywhere, the eye falls on signs of a happy family. Yet Mr. Khan lived through a nightmare that only recently came to an end. “The landlord wanted me to leave my apartment so he could do renovations and raise the rent.
Il essaie d’évincer tous les locataires: He’s trying to evict all the tenants who have lived in the building the longest,” says the father. He has lived in his Parc-Extension apartment for 22 years. His rent is the lowest in the building. Twice, the landlord tried to take him to court. “He had no real evidence against me, so he made up a bunch of lies. He told me he wanted to take back my apartment for his son and his partner, which wasn’t true,” the man says. Two of his neighbours, who have almost as much seniority as he does, are suffering the same fate.
M.Khan nous raconte qu’à maintes reprise: Mr. Khan tells us that on many occasions, the landlord showed up at his home unannounced to intimidate him. In a video he filmed – which was used as evidence in court – the landlord can be seen walking into his bathroom and criticizing the place. “Who lives like this?
On est au Canada, ici, pas au Bangladesh: This is Canada, not Bangladesh!” he can be heard exclaiming. The tenant believes it was an intimidation tactic meant to make him leave, on the pretext that his apartment was too run-down to live in. The building’s owner insisted that everything had to be renovated, even though, in more than 20 years, the father had never had a problem with the condition of his home. You immediately feel comfortable and welcome there. Mr. Khan’s landlord didn’t seem to see it that way. After repeating, on a video recording, that the family was living in unacceptable conditions, he went even further by criticizing tenants’ rights and claiming that landlords are kings.
« Il se croit tellement intelligent, ave: “He thinks he’s so smart, with his video camera. I know plenty of people like him, who think they’re super smart. So go ahead and film, who cares!” the landlord exclaims. The landlord then tried to send his lawyers to Mr. Khan’s home to get him to sign an agreement stating that he was obliged to move out. “I want to stay here. My kids go to school across the street. Everything is close to me,” he argues.
CAPE also came to the aid of Mr. Khan and his family, as well as the other tenants in the building who found themselves in the same situation. “They informed us about the steps to follow in this kind of situation,” the man says. He then gathered all the video evidence and the documents detailing the threats and lies made by his landlord.
Après avoir pris connaissance du dossier: After reviewing the file, the judge ruled in Mr. Khan’s favour. It was an enormous relief for the family after several years of stress. “I’m so grateful to CAPE, they’ve given me so much. They advised me and offered solutions. They check everything that’s wrong in a building and get in touch with the Administrative Housing Tribunal,” says Mr. Khan. Today, Mr. Khan is happy to share his experience with other tenants who find themselves in the same situation.
« Je dis à tout le monde qui est dans ce: “I tell everyone who’s in this kind of situation to gather evidence, especially videos, audio recordings or documents that can be given to the Administrative Housing Tribunal,” he urges. These documents will also be useful to the lawyer. “If the landlord doesn’t want you to film, you can tell him you need it as evidence. You have to try to negotiate with the landlord and be polite, otherwise it can be held against you. You can’t give up.”
Tout près, dans un immeuble de la rue de: Nearby, in a building on de l’Épée Street, tenants mobilized to stand up to a landlord who was making threats against them. Joining forces, they also turned to CAPE. Over the course of meetings held in the organization’s office, several of these tenants were able to get help from Alexandre Romanov, a lawyer specializing in housing. “People came together and there were victories. The landlord lost because he was doing whatever he pleased,” says Rizwan Khan, a CAPE community worker.
Devant la station de métro Parc, un imme: In front of the Parc metro station, a building at the corner of Hutchison Street and Ogilvy Avenue was also saved thanks to citizen action. The Plaza Hutchison, which housed community organizations and small local businesses, very nearly disappeared. “It was bought by real estate developers who wanted to turn it into condominiums,” explains Mr. Khan. “There was a huge mobilization in the neighbourhood, and a lot of political pressure.”
À la suite des mouvements solidaires, le: Following the solidarity movements, the owner ended up selling the building to the City of Montréal for $8M. Taken off the private market, the property is expected to be converted into social housing.
À Pointe-Saint-Charles, la mobilisation: In Pointe-Saint-Charles, the citizen mobilization that began 20 years ago ended in another victory this spring. Despite the pandemic, the warm atmosphere is still there at Bâtiment 7, where activities, though slowed, continue. Formerly owned by Canadian National, the vast industrial site has housed a self-managed centre since 2018 that hosts multiple projects. Auto mechanics, a library, artistic practices, a grocery store, a microbrewery and soon an early childhood centre (CPE) – the place benefits the community thanks to the project’s members and residents.
« Le B7 est un projet d’autogestion, c’e: “B7 is a self-management project, it’s a commons. You can go there to set up a project, or contribute to a project that’s already there,” explains Judith Cayer, a project manager and neighbourhood resident. However, the road was strewn with obstacles before citizens could take ownership of the space. In 2006, the land, with an area of 8.2 km2, was sold for $1 to a real estate developer.
À la suite d’une mobilisation citoyenne,: Following a citizen mobilization, the building was handed over to the community in 2012. More recently, the mobilization aimed at developing the outdoor spaces around the building, which were to be hemmed in by the construction of 60 condo buildings. The new agreement, signed last spring, provides for the development of community green spaces and the construction of 215 social and community housing units, as well as the distribution of the condos so as not to encircle the site. During this tug-of-war with the City and the developers, surprises kept piling up; the latest agreement on the development was originally supposed to be signed in 2012.
Joseph Bergeron, responsable du développ: Joseph Bergeron, head of outdoor project development, followed the project from the beginning before officially joining the organization. “We’re so proud that it finally broke through. Like all victories, it’s a story of perseverance, we’d been making these demands for a long time,” he says. It really did take a fight.
« Le promoteur ne se sentait pas d’oblig: “The developer didn’t feel any obligation toward the community,” says Mr. Bergeron. “It’s a solution that costs nobody anything, a development, but it took 10 years,” adds Ms. Cayer. Faced with the mobilization, elected officials decided to side with the community and to pressure the developer so that a development that benefits everyone would be carried out.
« Ils ont accepté d’écouter et de reconn: “They agreed to listen and to acknowledge that we had done our homework to propose a solution,” says Ms. Cayer. Time, allies and perseverance – those are the watchwords for citizens who want to change things. “If we keep demanding and following up on the files, we can end up winning,” says Judith Cayer. Joseph Bergeron also suggests getting to know people with different skills.
« Que ce soit pour donner un coup de mai: “Whether it’s to lend a hand with the legal side, or with construction, urban planning and architecture,” he says. Finally, he stresses the importance of innovating and arming yourself with patience to convince as many people as possible and, above all, of taking your demands to the political level. “It’s important to spread the word to our elected officials and to see what alliances we can forge. You have to insist and keep developing the project, whether or not you sense an openness; over time, the project will gain credibility.”
Comme Mme Cayer le décrit, Pointe-Saint-: As Ms. Cayer describes it, Pointe-Saint-Charles “is a neighbourhood where people say hello on the sidewalk and where everyone feels proud to live.” While there is a rather exceptional sense of community there, and a strong and active activist spirit, the resident hopes the government will put measures in place to deal with what she considers to be major gentrification of the neighbourhood.
« Que reste-t-il à faire, à part s’organ: “What’s left to do, other than organize?” It remains to be hoped that their demands will be heard.
